job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now my day is the same loop. I get up around eight in the rented room I share in Eastbury, make tea, then spend four or five hours on job sites and company portals. I finished a civil engineering degree in the summer, so I'm looking for junior engineer or technician jobs. After lunch I do a bit of tidying up my CV, and in the evening I stack shelves three nights a week at a supermarket to cover rent. It's tiring in a quiet way, because nothing is moving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you tell me a bit about the last few months of the search?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've sent about ninety applications since July. I've had two phone screens and one interview, with a drainage contractor called Pell and Marsh, where I did my eight-week internship. They said I was good but they had no headcount. I owe a lot in student loans, I've got maybe two weeks of living costs in the bank, and there's no help from home. My mum cleans offices in another city and she's got her own rent to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work, to be honest, I'd say I told you so to the people who said AI would take everything. If it's mostly hype, good. I'd still say the real problem isn't AI, it's firms that don't want to train anyone and put 'two years experience' on a junior job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my situation doesn't change, and my situation is bad. There are few civil jobs near Eastbury, my loan payments start soon, and a plateau means the same thin market I'm stuck in now. I'm not relieved so much as stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but wider. I'd try the council's highways team, the water company's graduate scheme and the rail contractors, which I've been too shy to chase. I'd keep the supermarket nights and ask the union rep there about more hours. I'd also go to the careers office at my old university, which I've been avoiding because I feel embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not frightening. It's like being in a queue that doesn't move. I'm angry more than scared, and a bit ashamed when my friends post about their first-day photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the shelf-stacking. What's the first thing you'd cut if the nights got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing to go would be my phone contract, then the train trips to see my mum. Food is last because I already eat cheaply. Honestly, rent is the thing that can't be cut, and that's what scares me, because one missed month and my landlord Mr Hanley will find someone else for the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for how hard it is to get a first job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the firms and the government. Companies make millions and still hire only people with contacts. And the government cut the apprenticeship money for engineering. I'd say if they want more engineers, they should pay firms to take juniors on, not leave graduates to sit in a room doing applications.

say: I'd say AI is **hype** and the real problem is firms refusing to train juniors.
I'd tell friends the government should pay firms to take on graduate engineers.
think: Privately, nothing improves for me, so I stay **stuck** in a thin local market.
Loan payments are coming and I have two weeks of money in the bank.
do: Apply **wider**, to the council highways team and the water company's graduate scheme.
Keep the three supermarket night shifts and ask the union rep for more hours.
Visit my university careers office, which I've avoided out of embarrassment.
feel: Angry and **stuck**, like a queue that never moves.
A bit ashamed when friends post first-day photos.
S0.quote: If they want more engineers, they should pay firms to take juniors on, not leave graduates to sit in a room doing applications.
fieldNote: He blames **employers** and government, not AI, which fits his left-leaning view.
**Shame** about the search is clear but he keeps trying; he is not frozen yet.
**Rent** and a landlord who could replace him are his real fear.

steps.text: Apply to the council highways team and the water company's graduate scheme
Ask the supermarket union rep for extra night shifts
Cancel the phone contract and cut the train trips to see mum
Book a visit to the university careers office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning, and I'd say workers need protection now, not later. If software is doing drawings, checking and planning, the junior engineers who used to learn from doing it are the first to go. I'd ask for rules that make firms keep training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. A graduate's first jobs are drawing up sections, checking levels, writing reports and chasing orders, and those are all thinking tasks. My internship at Pell and Marsh was mostly that. If that's gone, there's no ladder to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the engineers' union as a graduate member, which is cheap, and go to their meetings. I'd also apply for site technician and inspector jobs, because they're out in the mud and software can't do that yet. And I'd finally sit down and see what the drawing software now does, even though I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. I feel like the door is being shut slowly while I'm still looking for the handle. I don't have a cushion, so a few years of change is not just 'time to adjust' for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a junior civil engineer's work do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drafting, the quantity sums, the first-pass design checks and the report writing. At Pell and Marsh I did the take-offs, which means counting pipes and concrete from drawings, and I could see a program doing it in minutes. The site walks, the talking to the farmer whose field you're crossing, that part stays human for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd force myself to learn it, but as a tool I'm made to use, not because I like it. I don't trust it, and I don't like that firms will use it to cut people. But I'd rather be the junior who can check what the machine says than the one who loses to it.

I'd say workers need protection now, not later.
think: Junior work is thinking work, so my first rung may **vanish** while I'm still looking.

Apply for site technician and inspector jobs, which are outdoors and harder to automate.
Try the drawing software's new features, though I don't like them.

S1.quote: I feel like the door is being shut slowly while I'm still looking for the handle.
fieldNote: Sees **entry-level** work as the exposed layer, which matches the field.

Reluctance to learn AI softens into a **grudging** plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the street. I'd say governments must stop this or slow it, and we need a basic income and a say for workers before it's too late. Online I'd be shouting that nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm terrified, and I don't see how I come out of this. Two years is nothing. By the time I get a first job, if I do, AI can already do my job better and cheaper, and I haven't even paid off the loan for a degree that just became close to worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I could, move back in with my mum even though there's one bedroom and she works nights, and stop sending applications to jobs that won't exist. I'd put my name to every support scheme I can find and join protests. I really don't know what else. I don't have a plan, and that's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. It's like standing on a station platform watching the train arrive too fast, and knowing you left your ticket at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum the day this is announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my mum and say sorry, I did everything right and it still might not work. She'd say come home. I'd be saving her a month of rent by being there, and she'd say not to worry, but she'd lie awake like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning change anything you'd do about your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The loan is the same loan, and if my income never starts, the payments pile up. I'd have to ask the loan company about pausing it, and hope the rules change before I go under. Two years isn't enough for me to get ahead of it.

say: I'd join street protests and demand **limits** on the pace of AI and a basic income.
Online I'd say nobody voted for this.
think: Two years is nothing, and my degree may be **worthless** before I ever use it.
The student loan keeps growing even if I never earn.
do: Move back in with my **mum** to save rent, even in a one-bedroom flat.
Ask the loan company about pausing payments and apply for every support scheme.
Join protests and stop applying for jobs that won't exist.
feel: **Sick**, like watching a train arrive too fast without my ticket.
No **plan**, and I'm honest about that.
S2.quote: I'd call my mum and say sorry, I did everything right and it still might not work.
fieldNote: **Panic** comes from the loan, no cushion and no plan, not from drama.
Return to his mother's **one-bedroom** flat shows how little room he has.
**Politics** and protest fill the gap where a personal plan should be.

steps.text: Move back into mum's one-bedroom flat to save rent
Ask the loan company to pause payments
Join protests demanding a basic income
Stop sending applications to junior drainage jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to organise, but only if people start now. I'd tell friends to join a union and push their MPs. If we wait, firms will decide for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better than two years, but it's still the same wall. If I get a first job in the next year, I may have three or four years of experience before AGI, which is something. But the junior jobs I'd do are the ones that go first, so I'd be the first to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get any engineering job, even a poorly paid site technician post, so I have a name on a CV and a few years of pay to pay down the loan. I'd also take an evening course in surveying or health and safety, because humans still sign those off. I'd save every pound I could and keep the supermarket shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less panicky than two years, more like a long grey cloud. I can still see a route, but it's narrow and I'm not sure my boots fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year, easily. If I don't get in now, there's nothing to build on, and every month of nothing counts. By year four, the whole industry's worried, so at least I wouldn't be alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the next five years would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd get a job first and pay down the loan first. In the two-year world, I can't. Here I could pay off maybe a third of it, which would feel like climbing off a sinking boat with something in my pocket.

I'd push our local MP to back rules on AI hiring.
think: Even with five years, the junior jobs I'd do go first, so I'd be **first** out.
Any job now gives me a CV and some pay for the loan.

Sign up for an evening health and safety course, because people still sign those off.

fieldNote: Extra time brings a **plan**, but he still expects to be among the first cut.
Wants any job to build **savings** and a CV, not a dream role.
Health and safety **sign-off** is his idea of work that stays human.

steps.text: Accept any site technician job in the Eastbury area
Take an evening health and safety course
Put every spare pound toward the student loan
Keep the three weekly supermarket night shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like plenty, and I'd probably say it's a problem for later. At work I'd get on with things, but I'd still tell people we need the rules now because ten years goes fast, especially with a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the easiest of the five, but I'm still not comfortable. I'd have time to get a first job, build real experience and maybe get into something like site supervision, which should last. But I don't believe the end point is different. I'd still be on shaky ground at thirty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: more applications, more evening courses, and a proper professional membership once I get a job, because a title helps. I'd pay the loan down as fast as I could and hope to rent a flat of my own in a few years. I wouldn't change career yet. I'd watch and adjust around year seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the rest, although not calm. The worry's still there but there's room around it, like a long bridge instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still want to work in civil engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd want to go for the parts people need to see. Site work, inspection, talking to residents about a flood scheme. I picked civil because I like seeing something get built, and ten years gives me time to get good at the part that's slowest to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer, if you finally got one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be trained, properly, with someone sitting next to me for the first months. And a union that the firm talks to. If a firm says it's rolling out software, I'd want them to say who it replaces and what they'll do for those people, before it happens.

say: I'd say ten years sounds long but goes **fast**, and we need rules now.
I'd carry on with work as normal in public.
think: It's the easiest of the five, but I'd still be on **shaky** ground at thirty-three.
Time lets me build experience, ideally in site supervision.
do: Keep applying, take **evening** courses and get professional membership once I'm hired.
Pay the loan down fast, aiming for a flat of my own in a few years.
Review my career around year seven instead of changing now.
feel: **Calmer** than the other pictures but not calm.
Like a long **bridge** instead of a cliff.
S4.quote: I picked civil because I like seeing something get built, and ten years gives me time to get good at the part that's slowest to automate.
fieldNote: The extra decade turns fear into a workable **plan**, though debt still sets the mood.
He picks **site-facing** work, which matches his dislike of screen-first tools.
He expects to adjust at **year seven** instead of moving now.

steps.text: Take professional membership courses once a firm hires me
Pay the student loan down as fast as possible
Keep applying for junior roles in site supervision
Review the career plan again around year seven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years doesn't give me time to get a job, pay a loan or work out what I'd even be doing. What would help is boring: a pause on loan payments, a basic income if work disappears, and a rule that firms have to train juniors. Also somebody at the council or a union who actually answers an email.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy and we aren't stupid. We did the work and played by the rules. I'd like someone in charge to say plainly what they'll do for people at the bottom of the ladder, because from here it looks like nobody's planning for us.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't lazy and we aren't stupid. We did the work and played by the rules.
portrait: Zane is a **23-year-old** civil engineering graduate in Eastbury with a good degree, one internship and no offer after ninety applications.
He shares a rented room, stacks shelves three nights weekly and has about **two weeks** of costs saved.
He leans left, blames employers and government for the closed ladder, and hopes in unions and rules.
He never uses AI tools and only learns them grudgingly, so he moves **slowly** when things speed up.
His mood runs from anxious to panicked as warning time shrinks, easing only when ten years gives room for a plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because two years leaves no time to start a career or deal with the loan.
whatWouldHelp: A **pause** on loan payments, a basic income if work disappears, and rules that make firms train juniors.
